blocks.prompt: Ready to Go
blocks.text: Firefighters keep their gear right by the door. The boots stand open with the pants already around them. When the bell rings, they step in and pull everything on fast. The coat and pants are thick. Fire cannot burn through them. The helmet is hard, so falling things bounce off. On their back they carry a tank of air. The tank lets them breathe inside the smoke. Then they climb on the truck. The truck carries water, hoses, and a long ladder that can reach past a roof. The siren tells the cars to move out of the way. At the fire, they point the hose and the water pulls the heat away.

blocks.prompt: Why Firefighters Crawl
blocks.text: Fire is hungry. To keep burning it needs three things at once: something to burn, heat, and air. Take away any one of the three and the fire dies. That is the whole job. Water works because it soaks up heat. So much heat pours into the water that the fire has none left to keep itself going. Smoke is the other danger, and it does something strange. Hot smoke is lighter than cool air, so it rises. It spreads flat across the ceiling first, then fills the room downward, like a bathtub filling from the top. That means the cleanest, coolest air in a burning room is the air near the floor. This is why firefighters crawl. It is also why you should crawl if you ever smell smoke at home. Stay low, and go. One more thing. Firefighters wear a tank on their back, and most people think it holds oxygen. It does not. It holds ordinary air, squeezed in tight, the same air you are breathing right now.

blocks.prompt: Seventy Pounds and Three Minutes
blocks.text: Before a firefighter walks into a burning building, she puts on about seventy pounds of equipment. Coat and pants of flame-resistant fabric. Boots. Gloves. A hood over the ears and neck. A helmet. On her back, a tank of compressed air feeding a mask sealed against her face. She will do her work wearing all of it, in the dark, in heat that can curl the paint off a wall. She is racing a clock, and the clock has gotten faster. In the 1970s, a family in a burning home had roughly seventeen minutes to get out. Today the number is closer to three. Nothing about fire changed. Our furniture did. Older couches and chairs were built from wood, cotton, and wool. Modern ones are mostly plastic foam, and plastic foam is made from oil. Oil burns hot and fast. A living room today is a room full of solid gasoline. Two tools help. A thermal imaging camera turns heat into a picture, so a firefighter can see a hot spot through smoke that hides everything else. And a small device clipped to her coat quietly listens for movement. If she stops moving for thirty seconds, it screams, so the crew outside knows exactly where to dig.

blocks.prompt: The Job That Stopped Being About Fire
blocks.text: Ask a child what a firefighter does and the answer comes instantly: they put out fires. Ask a firefighter and the answer takes longer. In the United States, only a small share of the calls a fire department answers are fires. Most are medical. Someone's chest hurts. Someone fell in the shower. Someone's kid is not breathing right. The engine that arrives is often the closest trained help in the neighborhood, and it comes whether or not anything is burning. Most firefighters train as emergency medical technicians, and the tool they reach for most is not a hose. It is a medical bag. The job also runs on people who are not paid for it. Roughly two out of three firefighters in the country are volunteers, mostly in small towns. They have day jobs. A pager goes off in the middle of a shift or a dinner, and they leave. That is not a new idea. In 1736, Benjamin Franklin helped start one of the first organized volunteer fire companies in America, in Philadelphia. Neighbors bought their own leather buckets, marked them, and agreed to run to each other's houses. Around 1815, a woman named Molly Williams, who was enslaved, hauled an engine through a New York blizzard alongside Oceanus Engine Company 11, and is remembered as the first known female firefighter in the country. Even the shape of the helmet is old and practical. The long brim at the back was designed in 1836 by a man named Henry Gratacap, and it is not decoration. It keeps scalding water and falling embers off the back of a firefighter's neck. The fires that remain are worse than they used to be, which is why the training keeps growing. But the truth of the modern job is quieter than the picture painted on the truck. Most days, the worst thing in the room is not a flame. It is a person having the worst hour of their life, and somebody showed up.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Fire needs fuel, oxygen, and heat
Flashover: a whole room ignites at once
Flashover happens near 1,100 degrees Fahrenheit
Backdraft: a starved fire erupts when given air
Escape time fell from about 17 minutes to about 3
Most fire department calls today are medical

blocks.prompt: Flashover: The Three Minutes That Changed the Job
blocks.text: Everything that burns is doing one thing: coming apart in the presence of oxygen and throwing off heat as it goes. A fire needs fuel, oxygen, and enough heat to keep that reaction rolling. Remove any leg of the tripod and it stops. That is the entire theory. The practice is harder, because a burning room is not a campfire. It is a machine building toward one moment. Here is the moment. A couch catches. It burns in one corner and the room still looks survivable. Hot gas rises and layers along the ceiling, thickening downward, and that layer radiates heat back onto every surface below it: the carpet, the curtains, the coffee table, the second couch. None of those things are burning yet. They are being cooked. When their surfaces reach somewhere near eleven hundred degrees Fahrenheit, they stop behaving like furniture and start releasing flammable gas all at once, and the entire room ignites in a single breath. Firefighters call this flashover. Nothing in the room survives it. From first flame to flashover can be under four minutes. The clock used to be kinder. Testing in the 1970s suggested a family had roughly seventeen minutes to get out of a burning house. Recent testing by Underwriters Laboratories puts the figure closer to three. Fire did not change. Furniture did. A room once built from wood, cotton, wool, and horsehair is now built from polyurethane foam and plastic, both made from petroleum, and both release more energy, faster, with far more smoke. The modern living room is a fuel package with cushions on it. This is why ventilation is the most misunderstood tool on the fireground. Cutting a hole in a roof or breaking a window sounds like relief, and sometimes it is. But a fire in a sealed house is usually limited by oxygen long before it runs out of fuel, and handing a starved fire air is like blowing on coals. Open the wrong thing at the wrong second and the fire does not calm down. It inhales. In the worst case it answers with a backdraft, a sudden ignition that throws fire back out of the opening you just made. Research has turned old instincts inside out. Crews now often push water through a window from outside first, cooling the gas layer and buying the room back, and only then go in. For a century that would have been called cowardly. The evidence says it saves people, including the ones still inside. None of this makes the job safe. It makes it legible. The gear helps: roughly seventy pounds of flame-resistant fabric, a compressed-air tank, a sealed mask, a thermal imaging camera that renders invisible heat as a gray picture, an alarm that shrieks if the person wearing it goes still. But no gear lowers the temperature of a room. It only buys minutes. And here is the part that surprises people. Most of what a fire department does now has nothing to do with any of this. In the United States, the large majority of calls are medical rather than fires. The engine comes because it is close and its crew is trained, and the emergency is usually a person on a kitchen floor, not a wall of flame. The fire half of the job got rarer and, at the same time, deadlier. Everything else got bigger. The truck is still red, and the picture in everyone's head is still a hundred years old.
